facts.text: On this date in 1960, Cyprus gained independence from Britain — making it one of the youngest nations in Europe, yet home to one of the oldest cities on Earth: Nicosia, continuously inhabited for over 4,500 years.
On this date in 1977, Elvis Presley died in Memphis. The city's tourism economy now earns more annually from Graceland visitors than it did during his entire recording career.
Indonesia spans a wider longitude than the continental United States, yet shares no land border with any country except through its half of New Guinea island.
Monaco has a higher density of millionaires per capita than any other country — roughly one in three residents qualifies — yet it maintains its own military, staffed by roughly 250 people.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area houses 37 million people, more than the entire population of Canada, all served by a rail network so precise its average delay is measured in seconds per year.
On August 16, 1971, Nixon closed the gold window — ending Bretton Woods and untethering the dollar from gold forever. Every fiat currency in your wallet traces its birth to that weekend.
On this date in 1982, the Dow closed at 776. It would hit 36,000 by 2021 — a 46x return that made the 1982 entry point one of the greatest generational gifts in market history.
The S&P 500 has spent roughly 75% of all trading days below its all-time high. Sitting at a peak feels normal; statistically, it is the exception.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway once traded for $18 a share. The A-shares crossed $700,000 in 2024 — Buffett has never split them, on principle.
The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded corporation, paid an average annual dividend of 18% for nearly 200 years. It also went spectacularly bankrupt in 1799.

On this date in 1960, Joseph Kittinger stepped from a balloon at 102,800 feet and free-fell for 4 minutes 36 seconds, reaching 614 mph — becoming the first human to break the sound barrier without a vehicle.

On this date in 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope detected the 'Wow! signal' — a 72-second burst so perfectly matching expected extraterrestrial transmission patterns that the astronomer on duty wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. It has never been explained.
Your skeleton is not the rigid scaffold it feels like. Bone is living tissue that completely replaces itself roughly every decade, making the skeleton you were born with genuinely gone.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly 10 million tons on Earth.

The human eye can detect a single photon in complete darkness. Your visual system is not limited by your eyes — it is limited by your brain, which suppresses lone photon signals as noise to avoid phantom images.
On this day in 1977, Elvis Presley died — younger than the Rolling Stones are now.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
On this day in 1896, gold was discovered in the Klondike, launching a stampede that killed more men than it enriched.
The fax machine was invented before the telephone. Alexander Bain patented it in 1843; Bell's telephone came in 1876.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. It began around 1096; Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.

Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already in wider use than most century-old words.
Hiraeth (Welsh, n.): a longing for a home that no longer exists, or perhaps never did. Untranslatable precisely because English assumes you can return to what you miss.

On this date in 1858, Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged the first transatlantic telegraph messages. The word 'telegraphic' had existed for decades — suddenly it meant something planetary.
Kenopsia (n.): the eerie quiet of a place that is usually bustling — an empty school, a closed fair. Another Koenig coinage that filled a gap most people didn't know was there.
On August 16, 1977, Elvis Presley died, and obituaries reached for 'ineffable' — beyond words. From Latin ineffabilis, it originally applied only to things too sacred to be spoken aloud.
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin's SegWit upgrade activated at block 481,824 — ending a two-year civil war over block size and splitting the chain into BTC and Bitcoin Cash eight days later.
On August 16, 2012, BitcoinTalk user Pirateat40 collapsed a 700,000 BTC Ponzi — then the largest Bitcoin fraud — simply by stopping reply posts. No code exploit, no hack.
Ethereum's gas limit is set by miners and validators through informal signaling, not protocol votes. It has been raised over 20 times with zero on-chain governance formality.
The Bitcoin genesis block contains unspendable coins by design: Satoshi hardcoded the 50 BTC coinbase reward in a way that makes it provably unclaimable, a deliberate choice still debated.
Solana's 'proof of history' is not a consensus mechanism — it's a cryptographic clock. Consensus still runs on top via Tower BFT; most people conflate the two.

On this date in 2012, Google's 'cat neuron' paper hit arXiv — a 16,000-core cluster trained unsupervised on YouTube frames spontaneously developed a neuron responding selectively to cat faces, without ever being told cats existed.
On this date in 2018, OpenAI published the original GPT paper. The model had 117M parameters; six years later GPT-4 is estimated at over 1 trillion — a 10,000x scale increase in one half-decade.

AlphaFold2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially every catalogued protein known to science — in roughly 18 months, a task that would have taken conventional crystallography longer than the age of the universe.

The Chinchilla scaling paper (2022) showed that most large language models of its era were undertrained relative to their size: optimal compute splits tokens and parameters roughly 1-to-1, a result that retroactively made GPT-3 look wasteful.

Modern GPU clusters used for frontier model training dissipate enough heat that their power draw rivals mid-sized cities; the Frontier supercomputer at Oak Ridge peaks near 21 megawatts — comparable to powering 17,000 average US homes continuously.
